ourAnswer: Mn(2+) is 3d5, half-filled and extra stable; oxidation to Mn(3+) = 3d4 destroys it, so the third ionisation enthalpy of Mn is very high. Fe(2+) = 3d6 goes to the stable half-filled Fe(3+) = 3d5, so it is oxidised easily.
keyAnswer: It is because Mn(2+) has 3d5 configuration which has extra stability.
note: Same reason. Ours additionally supplies the Fe side of the comparison (3d6 to 3d5 is favourable) and the electrode potentials, which the key omits.

ourAnswer: 3d3 (V): +2, +3, +4, +5, stable +4/+5. 3d5 (Mn): +2 to +7, most stable +2. 3d8 (Ni): +2. 3d4: no neutral first-series atom has this ground state, since Cr is 3d5 4s1; taking the atom as Cr the stable state is +3.
keyAnswer: 3d3 (Vanadium): (+2), +3, +4, +5. 3d5 (Chromium): +3, +4, +6. 3d5 (Manganese): +2, +4, +6, +7. 3d8 (Nickel): +2, +3 (in complexes). 3d4: there is no d4 configuration in the ground state.
note: Agrees everywhere our answer speaks, including the sharpest part — the key's closing line 'there is no d4 configuration in the ground state' is exactly the point our answer and its _note make. TWO INCOMPLETENESSES ON OUR SIDE, both worth the maintainer's eye and neither an error. (a) The key reads '3d5' as ambiguous between CHROMIUM (3d5 4s1) and MANGANESE (3d5 4s2) and answers BOTH; we answered only manganese. Our solution does state that Cr's ground state is 3d5 4s1, but uses it under the 3d4 heading rather than also listing Cr under 3d5. (b) The key adds Ni +3 'in complexes', which we did not mention. Nothing we wrote is contradicted.

keyAnswer: Vanadate VO3(-), chromate CrO4(2-), permanganate MnO4(-)
note: Chromate and permanganate identical. The vanadate differs in FORM ONLY and both are correct: metavanadate VO3(-) gives V = +5 (x - 6 = -1) and orthovanadate VO4(3-) gives V = +5 (x - 8 = -3), so both satisfy 'oxidation state equal to the group number', 5. Not a defect on either side. Worth recording that the CHAPTER'S OWN section 4.4.1 (page 16, 0-based) uses our form, printing 'V2O5 ... gives VO4(3-) as well as VO2(+) salts', so a student following the chapter text would write VO4(3-) and be marked against a key that prints VO3(-).

ourAnswer: +3 for every lanthanoid (characteristic); in addition +2 (Sm, Eu, Yb; Tm in solids) and +4 (Ce, Pr, Nd, Tb, Dy, only Ce(4+) important in solution), arising where 4f0, 4f7 or 4f14 results.
keyAnswer: +3 is the common oxidation state of the lanthanoids. In addition to +3, oxidation states +2 and +4 are also exhibited by some of the lanthanoids.
note: Identical content; ours names which elements and gives the 4f0/4f7/4f14 reason the key leaves out.

ourAnswer: Transition: successive states differ by UNITY (V(II) to V(V); Mn +2 to +7). Non-transition: differ by TWO because of the inert pair effect (Sn2+/Sn4+, Pb2+/Pb4+, Tl+/Tl3+).
keyAnswer: In transition elements the oxidation states vary from +1 to any highest oxidation state by one, e.g. manganese +2 to +7. In the nontransition elements the variation is selective, always differing by 2, e.g. +2, +4, or +3, +5 or +4, +6.
note: Same distinction, same manganese example. Ours names the inert pair effect as the cause and adds the group-direction contrast (Mo(VI)/W(VI) more stable than Cr(VI)).

ourAnswer: Coloured: Ti(3+) 3d1, V(3+) 3d2, Mn(2+) 3d5 (very pale), Fe(3+) 3d5, Co(2+) 3d7. COLOURLESS: Sc(3+) 3d0 AND Cu(+) 3d10.
keyAnswer: Except Sc(3+), all others will be coloured in aqueous solution because of incompletely filled 3d-orbitals, will give rise to d-d transitions.
note: The key names ONE exception where there are TWO: it implies Cu(+) is coloured. Cu(+) is [Ar]3d10 — a COMPLETELY filled d subshell with no vacancy for an electron to be promoted into, so no d-d transition is possible and it is colourless. THE KEY CONTRADICTS ITSELF IN ITS OWN SENTENCE: the reason it gives, 'because of incompletely filled 3d-orbitals', is precisely the criterion that EXCLUDES Cu(+), while its scope, 'except Sc(3+), all others', includes it. Two further independent confirmations from the chapter itself: (1) section 4.3.10 (page 14, 0-based) states the mechanism as an electron 'excited from a lower energy d orbital to a higher energy d orbital', impossible for d10; (2) the chapter's own Table 4.8 on the same page lists every d0 and d10 species as colourless — 3d0 Sc(3+) colourless, 3d0 Ti(4+) colourless, 3d10 Zn(2+) colourless — and Cu(+) has the identical 3d10 configuration to that last entry. The key should read 'Except Sc(3+) and Cu(+)'.

ourAnswer: (i) Cr(2+) d4 to d3 = t2g3, maximum CFSE, so reducing; Mn(III) d4 to d5 half-filled, so oxidising. (ii) A strong-field ligand gives a large splitting and low-spin Co(III) d6 = t2g6 acquires a very large CFSE, stabilising +3 over +2 and dropping E° from about +1.8 V to about +0.1 V. (iii) A d1 ion has one loosely held electron and is one electron from the stable d0 configuration, so it is readily oxidised (Ti(3+) to Ti(4+), V(4+) to V(5+)).
keyAnswer: (i) Cr(2+) is reducing as it involves change from d4 to d3, the latter is more stable (t2g3); Mn(III) to Mn(II) is 3d4 to 3d5, again extra stable. (ii) Due to CFSE, which more than compensates the 3rd IE. (iii) The hydration or lattice energy more than compensates the ionisation enthalpy involved in removing the electron from d1.
note: (i) and (ii) identical, ours quantified. (iii) states the SAME CONCLUSION by a different and complementary route: the key gives the energetic half (hydration/lattice energy pays for the ionisation enthalpy), ours gives the configurational half (the drive to reach d0). Both are standard and neither contradicts the other, but ours is the less complete of the two and omits the thermodynamic compensation the key names — recorded for the maintainer as an incompleteness, not an error.

ourAnswer: Copper. Cu is [Ar]3d10 4s1, so losing the single 4s electron gives Cu(+) = [Ar]3d10, a stable completely filled subshell.
keyAnswer: Copper, because with +1 oxidation state an extra stable configuration, 3d10 results.
note: Identical.

ourAnswer: Mn(3+) = 4, Cr(3+) = 3, V(3+) = 2, Ti(3+) = 1 unpaired electrons; most stable in aqueous solution is Cr(3+).
keyAnswer: Unpaired electrons Mn(3+) = 4, Cr(3+) = 3, V(3+) = 2, Ti(3+) = 1. Most stable Cr(3+).
note: Exact match on all five parts. Ours adds the reason for Cr(3+) (t2g3, maximum CFSE in the octahedral aqua field).

ourAnswer: Inner transition elements are the f-block, in which the last electron enters an (n-2)f orbital. Of the six given, 59 (Pr), 95 (Am) and 102 (No) are inner transition elements; 29 (Cu), 74 (W) and 104 (Rf) are d-block.
keyAnswer: Second part 59, 95, 102.
note: Exact match on the numbers. The key answers only the second part and leaves the definition unanswered, which it flags itself by writing 'Second part'.

ourAnswer: Lawrencium, Lr, Z = 103; [Rn]5f14 6d1 7s2; oxidation state +3 only, since the filled 5f14 core is unavailable and only the 6d1 and 7s2 electrons can be lost.
keyAnswer: Lawrencium, 103, +3
note: Exact match. The key gives no configuration; ours supplies it, which the question asks for.

ourAnswer: Ti(2+) 3d2, V(2+) 3d3, Cr(3+) 3d3, Mn(2+) 3d5, Fe(2+) 3d6, Fe(3+) 3d5, Co(2+) 3d7, Ni(2+) 3d8, Cu(2+) 3d9; all high-spin octahedral in water, t2g/eg occupancies given.
note: Exact match on all nine electron counts. The key answers only the first part of the question and prints nothing for the second (how the five 3d orbitals are occupied in the hydrated octahedral ions), which our answer supplies. The key's 'CO(2+)' is a typographic slip for cobalt Co(2+) — capital O for lowercase o — and its value 7 is correct, so it is a print defect with no effect on the answer.

ourAnswer: 2.2 BM -> n = 1: Mn(II) d5, low spin, CN- strong field. 5.3 BM -> n = 4: Fe(II) d6, high spin, H2O weak field. 5.9 BM -> n = 5: Mn(II) d5, high spin, Cl- weak field (tetrahedral).
keyAnswer: sqrt(n(n+2)) = 2.2, n approx 1, d2sp3, CN- strong ligand; = 5.3, n approx 4, sp3d2, H2O weak ligand; = 5.9, n approx 5, sp3, Cl- weak ligand.
note: The three values of n agree exactly (1, 4, 5) and so do all three ligand-field assignments (CN- strong, H2O weak, Cl- weak). The only difference is vocabulary: the key describes the structures with valence-bond hybridisation labels (d2sp3 / sp3d2 / sp3) while ours uses crystal-field language (low-spin t2g5 / high-spin t2g4eg2 / high-spin tetrahedral). These describe the same three structures — d2sp3 IS the low-spin octahedral case and sp3d2 the high-spin one — and the crystal-field vocabulary is the one this chapter itself uses in section 4.3.9, hybridisation belonging to Unit 5.

ourAnswer: Ag also shows +2 (AgF2, AgO), and Ag(2+) = [Kr]4d9 has an incompletely filled d subshell; the IUPAC definition covers the ions as well as the atom.
keyAnswer: Silver (Z = 47) can exhibit +2 oxidation state wherein it will have incompletely filled d-orbitals (4d), hence a transition element.
note: Identical. ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.

ourAnswer: Zn is 3d10 4s2; the filled 3d subshell has no unpaired electrons and takes no part in metallic bonding, so only the two 4s electrons bind the lattice and the interatomic interaction is the weakest in the series.
keyAnswer: In the formation of metallic bonds, no electrons from 3d-orbitals are involved in case of zinc, while in all other metals of the 3d series, electrons from the d-orbitals are always involved in the formation of metallic bonds.
note: Identical mechanism. (The key prints 'eletrons' for 'electrons' — a print defect in the key, no effect on the answer.) ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.

ourAnswer: Manganese, [Ar]3d5 4s2, which has the maximum number of unpaired electrons in the series; all seven valence electrons are of comparable energy, so every state from +2 to +7 is accessible.
keyAnswer: Manganese (Z = 25), as its atom has the maximum number of unpaired electrons.
note: Identical. ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.

ourAnswer: The high enthalpy of atomisation and high sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies of copper are not compensated by the hydration enthalpy of Cu(2+), so the overall free-energy change is positive and E° comes out positive.
note: The in-chapter intext key deliberately skips 4.4 (and 4.8) — its heading says 'Answers to SOME Intext Questions'. Not a defect. This row and 4.8 are therefore the only two intext rows in the chapter that ARE genuinely blind.

ourAnswer: The differing stability of the resulting 3d configurations — d0, d5 and d10 being exceptionally stable — superimposed on the general rise in effective nuclear charge. Cr and Cu have anomalously high second ionisation enthalpies (Cr(+) is 3d5, Cu(+) is 3d10) and Mn an anomalously low one (Mn(2+) is 3d5).
keyAnswer: Irregular variation of ionisation enthalpies is mainly attributed to varying degree of stability of different 3d-configurations (e.g., d0, d5, d10 are exceptionally stable).
note: Same cause, same three configurations named. Ours works it out element by element. ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.

ourAnswer: Oxygen and fluorine are the smallest and most electronegative elements, so they can oxidise the metal to its highest state and pack in large numbers around it; oxygen additionally forms p-pi d-pi multiple bonds, which is why the highest Mn fluoride is MnF4 while the highest oxide is Mn2O7.
keyAnswer: Because of small size and high electronegativity oxygen or fluorine can oxidise the metal to its highest oxidation state.
note: Same two reasons (small size, high electronegativity); ours adds the multiple-bonding point that distinguishes oxygen from fluorine. ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.

ourAnswer: Cr(2+). Its oxidation is d4 to d3 = t2g3, the maximum CFSE available to a high-spin ion, whereas Fe(2+) goes d6 to d5 which has zero CFSE in a weak field. E° values confirm it: -0.41 V against +0.77 V.
keyAnswer: Cr(2+) is stronger reducing agent than Fe(2+). Reason: d4 to d3 occurs for Cr(2+) to Cr(3+), but d6 to d5 for Fe(2+) to Fe(3+); in a medium like water d3 is more stable than d5 (see CFSE).
note: Identical, including the CFSE argument the key points at. ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.

ourAnswer: Z = 27 is Co, so Co(2+) = [Ar]3d7 with 3 unpaired electrons; mu = sqrt(3 x 5) = sqrt(15) = 3.87 BM.
note: The in-chapter key skips 4.8. Together with 4.4 this is one of only two genuinely blind intext rows. Independently checkable: the chapter's own Table 4.7 (page 13, 0-based) prints the calculated moment for 3d7 as 3.87 BM, which matches our answer exactly.

ourAnswer: Cu(+) disproportionates: 2Cu(+)(aq) -> Cu(2+)(aq) + Cu(s). The much more negative hydration enthalpy of the smaller, doubly charged Cu(2+) more than pays for the second ionisation enthalpy of copper, so the free-energy change is negative.
keyAnswer: Cu(+) in aqueous solution undergoes disproportionation, i.e., 2Cu(+)(aq) -> Cu(2+)(aq) + Cu(s). The E° value for this is favourable.
note: Same equation and same conclusion; ours supplies the hydration-enthalpy reason behind the key's 'the E° value is favourable'. (The key prints 'underoes' for 'undergoes' — a print defect, no effect on the answer.) ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.

ourAnswer: 5f orbitals are more diffuse and penetrate the core less than 4f, so they shield the nuclear charge more poorly; the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons therefore rises more steeply per element and the size shrinks more per element.
keyAnswer: The 5f electrons are more effectively shielded from nuclear charge. In other words the 5f electrons themselves provide poor shielding from element to element in the series.
note: Agrees with the key's operative claim, its second sentence. Worth flagging for the maintainer that the key's two sentences are NOT restatements of one another as its 'in other words' asserts: being well shielded is a different proposition from shielding others poorly. Both facts are true and both appear in the chapter (page 24, 0-based, states the 5f electrons are more effectively shielded), but only the second one explains the greater contraction, and that is the one our answer rests on. Not a defect, a loose connective. ⚠ NOT BLIND — see _META.
